item.description: PCSD and FBI investigators are examining a possible new ransom note in the kidnapping case involving Savannah Guthrie's mother, Nancy Guthrie, in Arizona.
item.content:encoded:
The Pima County Sheriff's Department (PCSD) announced Tuesday that PCSD and the FBI's task force investigating the disappearance of Savannah Guthrie's mother, Nancy, have been made aware of a possible new ransom note in relation to Guthrie's disappearance.

"The PCSD/FBI Guthrie Task Force was recently made aware of a new possible ransom note related to the Nancy Guthrie investigation," PCSD wrote in a Tuesday post on X.

"Investigators are also aware of social media comments regarding the note and are looking further into the information to determine its credibility," the post concluded.

NANCY GUTHRIE'S SUSPECTED ABDUCTION: TIMELINE OF EVENTS IN DISAPPEARANCE OF 'TODAY' HOST'S MOM

A law enforcement source close to the case tells Fox News there are no new notes being treated as credible.

Nancy Guthrie was taken from her Tucson, Arizona, home in the early hours of Feb. 1 and hasn't been seen since, according to the FBI and PCSD.

Guthrie was last seen shortly before 10 p.m. local time on Jan. 31 after a relative dropped her off at her home in the Catalina Foothills neighborhood of Tucson.

NANCY GUTHRIE CASE: UNCLAIMED $1.2M REWARD SUGGESTS 'VERY SMALL CIRCLE' OF SUSPECTS, RETIRED FBI AGENT SAYS

Authorities have struggled to identify a suspect or person of interest in her disappearance, despite a masked man appearing on Guthrie's Ring doorbell camera.

Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos, in the days following Guthrie's disappearance, confirmed that she was taken, telling reporters during a news briefing, "She did not leave on her own. We know that."

NANCY GUTHRIE INVESTIGATORS SEE UPTICK IN TIPS AFTER RANSOM NOTES RELEASE: SHERIFF

Authorities had previously released two ransom notes related to Guthrie's kidnapping in July.

The first, which was sent on Feb. 2, reported that Guthrie was unharmed and demanded that her captors be sent $4 million in cryptocurrency to secure her release.

NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM NOTES MAY BE FAKE AS RENOWNED PROFILER SAYS CASE LOOKS MORE LIKE BURGLARY GONE WRONG

The second, sent four days later on Feb. 6, said Guthrie had died shortly after she was kidnapped.

Authorities released the ransom notes in late July, noting they were written with a unique writing style, asking anyone who recognizes the patterns to share any information with PCSD and the FBI.

Anyone with information is asked to dial 1-800-CALL-FBI or, to remain anonymous, call 520-88-CRIME.

item.title: ‘Superman’ star Christopher Reeve’s son reveals 'shock' cancer diagnosis at age 34
item.description: Will Reeve, son of Christopher Reeve, revealed his embryonal carcinoma diagnosis and orchiectomy on air, drawing parallels to his parents' battles.
item.content:encoded:
Will Reeve, son of the late famed "Superman" actor Christopher Reeve, announced that he recently battled cancer.

The "Good Morning America" correspondent, 34, shared during Tuesday’s show that he was diagnosed with testicular cancer earlier this year, assuring viewers that he is "OK."

"The diagnosis was a shock and the treatments were a slog," he said. "Today, though, I am relieved to announce that we arrived at our destination and this cancer is in the rearview mirror. But what a journey."

WILLIAM SHATNER SAYS DOCTOR DISMISSED KEY WARNING SIGN BEFORE STAGE 4 CANCER DIAGNOSIS

Reeve said he found a "hard, tender lump in [his] left testicle" just a few months after his wedding to luxury event planner Amanda Dubin.

An ultrasound revealed that he had "a mass that had to come out." After undergoing surgery to remove the testicle (an orchiectomy), Reeve discovered the mass was embryonal carcinoma.

The aggressive subtype of testicular cancer can spread more quickly than some other forms, according to the American Cancer Society.

POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY PLAY SURPRISING ROLE IN CANCER OUTCOMES

Reeve later underwent a second surgery to remove lymph nodes from his abdomen after some cancer cells had spread there.

The surgery took place at Memorial Sloan Kettering, which is where his mother, Dana Reeve, died from lung cancer in 2006 at age 44. His father died in 2004 at the age of 52.

Reeve shared that he also underwent two rounds of chemotherapy to lower the risk that the cancer would return. He said he experienced several side effects from the medication, including ringing in the ears, bone pain, night sweats, blood clots and constant headaches.

He did not lose his hair because he used a method called "cold capping," which is used during certain chemotherapy treatments to help reduce hair loss by cooling the scalp and constricting blood vessels.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

After finishing his second round of chemotherapy on July 31, Reeve said he received "clean scans" on Sept. 8.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

In an interview with People, Reeve said he is "going to be fine," although it has been "one heck of a chapter."

"I’m fortunate that I caught this early," he said. "Yes, I had to jump through some flaming hoops to get to the other side, but it could have been much worse had I ignored it or delayed going to the doctor."

Reeve also praised his wife for serving as his "caregiver," similar to how his mother helped care for his father after a 1995 horseback-riding accident left him paralyzed.

"I learn[ed] more about what it was like to be my dad in the final nine years of his life, where he had my mom and our family taking care of him," Reeve said.

He added that the experience taught him how to "repurpose [adversity] into something hopeful."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Testicular cancer is among the most treatable cancers, particularly when detected early, according to the American Cancer Society. Experts recommend seeing a doctor promptly for any lump, swelling, pain or change in a testicle.

Fox News Digital reached out to Reeve’s representatives requesting comment.

item.title: Office of Personnel Management uncovers $500M in fraud and waste in federal health benefits programs
item.description: The Trump administration's Office of Personnel Management uncovered $510 million in fraud and waste across federal employee health benefits programs.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration announced $500 million in waste and fraud findings at the Office of Personnel Management – revealing a recovery of potentially fraudulent funds for federal health benefits programs.

Health insurance carriers in the Federal Employees Health Benefits and Postal Service Health Benefits programs reported preventing nearly $510 million in losses before or during payment and recovering an additional $21.9 million after claims were paid, according to the Office of Personnel Management.

"OPM runs health insurance for about 8.9 million retirees and federal employees, and we spend about $80 billion a year," Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor told Fox News Digital. "The $500 million, a little more than half percent, is a good number, but certainly we have a long way to go here to root out more fraud, waste and abuse."

FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP ADMIN OPENS NEW FRONT IN FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETING HEALTH INSURERS, DRUG MIDDLEMEN

The White House anti-fraud task force led by Vice President JD Vance has reported $260.7 billion in fraud uncovered since Trump took office, and $72 billion in fraud stopped on an annualized basis.

Kupor said his agency is conducting its own review of health insurance claims data for the first time, allowing the agency to analyze billing patterns across providers and health plans to identify unusual prescribing habits, surgery rates and other anomalies that could signal overuse, misuse or potential fraud.

TRUMP ADMIN BLOCKS MORE THAN $1.6B IN POTENTIALLY IMPROPER MEDICARE LAB PAYMENTS, AGENCY SAYS

He said the agency will use those findings to remove providers from federal health programs when warranted and will refer cases involving suspected criminal conduct to the agency’s Office of Inspector General and the Justice Department for further investigation.

Kupor leads the agency responsible for overseeing the federal workforce while managing key employment and benefits programs for millions of current and former federal employees. One of the most prominent examples of his work stems from Elon Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency’s (DOGE) targeting of a mine in Pennsylvania.

EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE THE SECRETIVE MINE DOGE HELPED DRAG OUT OF A DECADES-OLD BUREAUCRATIC BLACK HOLE

Last April, Fox News Digital first reported that the United States government applied the use of artificial intelligence for federal employee recordkeeping – the first time the federal government implemented AI at scale.

The movement was led by Kupor and Musk, and Musk didn’t hide his shock that federal records were being stored and managed solely on paper at the time.

TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’

"The speed at which the mine shaft elevator can move determines how many people can retire... And the elevator breaks down and then nobody can retire," Musk said last February. "Doesn't that sound crazy?"

When asked for an update on progress made on modernizing the mine, Kupor said it is now fully operational on an electronic system.

"This past year, we did 180,000 electronic online applications for retirement, which is just unprecedented," he said. "That's almost double the production that we've had in any prior year. Electronic applications can get solved in less than half the time today that a paper one does."

"We will take something that has been a six-month, nine-month, 12-month horrendous process for retirees, and I think we will be able to do it in as little as 15 days with the continued development of technology."

WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE

Kupor’s previous experience working with artificial intelligence has led to his name being floated to serve as the AI czar in the Trump administration – a role cast into the spotlight as data center development and artificial intelligence have become midterm election talking points.

After working as an investment banker at Credit Suisse, Kupor worked at Loudcloud, which was co-founded by Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, in 1999. He was then hired as the first employee by Andreessen and Horowitz at the duo’s venture capital firm. Kupor also served as the chair of the National Venture Capital Association from May 2017 to May 2018.

TRUMP SAYS ANTI-FRAUD EFFORTS ARE UNCOVERING BILLIONS IN WASTE, CLAIMS SAVINGS COULD BALANCE BUDGET

When asked about whether he has had any conversations with the White House about the role, Kupor said he had seen the reports he was being floated, and discussed President Donald Trump’s views on artificial intelligence broadly.

"I’ve read all the same reports you've read and don't have anything to add there," he said. "What the president has said is exactly 100% right, which is that AI is the most important piece of technology that will determine economic growth for us, national security, sovereignty for our country."

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION UNCOVERS $1.2B IN SUSPECTED COVID CONTRACT FRAUD TIED TO BIDEN-ERA SPENDING

"One of the things that I know, again, having spent all my life in the venture world, is there is no limit to the intellect and inventiveness of entrepreneurs in this country. And we just need to make sure that the conditions around, you know, regulatory controls and others continue to allow the U.S. to flourish in the way that it's always done."

Kupor did not rule out accepting the role if Trump should offer it to him, saying that while he is focused on his job as director of the agency, he serves "at the will of the president."

Reports had suggested that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was being considered for the AI czar position, but last week Trump said he would not be selecting him for the role.

item.title: Bucks go toe-to-toe in man's yard, manage to avoid his truck & boat during antler-locking combat
item.description: Bucks go antlers-to-antlers in a deer whisperer's yard as deer rut season approaches, sparring dangerously close to his parked truck and boat.
item.content:encoded:
It's that time of year when bucks are out preparing to establish their dominance in hopes of catching the eye of the does in the area. They square up with one another whenever and wherever the mood hits.

A couple of bucks decided to go toe-to-toe or antlers-to-antlers, if you will, in the yard of Lynn Smith, who calls himself a "deer whisperer." His yard, as he shares on Instagram, is often covered in deer.

With the rut approaching, these bucks are using his yard to do some sparring. All he asks as he documents these backyard brawls is that they leave the truck and the boat alone.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

It's not too much to ask from a guy who allows and even encourages the wild animals to roam around on his property. They do fight near the truck, but politely avoid doing any damage to it or the boat.

Now for the non-deer whisperers out there, you don't want to get too close to this kind of action, especially in peak rutting season when the horned-up bucks are cranking the battles up a couple of notches.

HIKER IN COLORADO TAKES TRIP TO THE HOSPITAL AFTER BEING KICKED IN THE BACK BY A MOOSE

The truck and the boat probably aren’t safe during that time of year either. The bucks aren't playing around and will do some damage to anything that is in the area. I'd assume that anyway. I don't have a yard full of deer.

Nor do I have bucks squaring up to do battle either. They could have some sort of understanding with the deer whisperer in place, for all I know.

I doubt it and I wouldn’t get too close to the action myself. Getting tangled up in antlers isn't my idea of an enjoyable afternoon.

item.title: Ross Chastain calls Ryan Blaney's fight with Carson Hocevar at Bristol Motor Speedway 'NASCAR 101'
item.description: Ross Chastain called the Ryan Blaney and Carson Hocevar fight at Bristol Motor Speedway "NASCAR 101," referenced it to the 1979 Daytona 500 brawl.
item.content:encoded:
While Joey Logano celebrated at Bristol Motor Speedway last week, Ryan Blaney went to fight Carson Hocevar.

Blaney, ticked off after finishing 33rd following a crash that resulted from contact with Hocevar’s car, took a couple of swings at Hocevar. NASCAR star Ross Chastain called the incident "NASCAR 101."

"But seeing Ryan be upset and go to Carson and seeing Carson defend himself when he gets grabbed, I think that's NASCAR 101. I think that's what's made our sport," Chastain told OutKick in a recent interview.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Chastain referenced the infamous fight between Cale Yarborough and Donnie Allison at the end of the 1979 Daytona 500 as a moment when the sport took off. Chastain said that fight had a lot more "horsepower behind it" than Blaney and Hocevar’s dust-up.

The driver of the No. 1 car said NASCAR security decides whether to break up a fight.

"I was glad to watch it, and I think security did a good job to let it happen, but then, NASCAR security gets to decide what they want to do and they decide to step in when they think it's time," Chastain told OutKick.

Chastain said he had no idea what was happening in the moment or whether Blaney had intended to go after Hocevar from the moment the crash happened.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"No, I have no idea. I don't think Carson had any idea that Ryan would be coming over there like that. I don't even know if Ryan really knew 'cause he had some time to think about it. He had to go to the care center, do interviews, walk back over to the holler, and then he waited on the race stand and walked over," Chastain said.

Chastain has been in a few fights, and while they are part of the fabric of the sport, he said he hopes his fighting days are over.

"It won't take much of a YouTube search to see. I've had my fair share of (fights) as well. I'm not saying anybody should fight, and, and I hope — I'm 33. I hope my fighting days are long behind me. Because getting punched is not something that I ever want to feel again. I don't want to feel that. I've made it to a spot in life where I hope I'm done with it," Chastain said.

After a race, Chastain would much rather drink a beer than get into a fight.

"There's bad races where we crash, we're out early, and it's like, you know what, the work's done. All the prep, all the focus, all the pressure of racing in the Cup Series is done. OK, let's have a beer. Let's just take a moment. All right, let's get out of here. Now, we're loaded up, we're done, done with the weekend. I'll rehydrate later," Chastain said on behalf of Busch Light.

"Then in the wins, definitely a Busch Light. And that's where you see me as soon as physically possible when I get out of the car and I'm done driving, that's when I want it. I'm hollering at my crew to bring me a beer. I don't want to even walk to the cooler. I want, as soon as I get out, I wanna have one 'cause the work's done. And, and if we've won, that's a big reward."

Busch Light is releasing limited-edition hunting cans for the 20th anniversary of the fan-favorite hunting cans. Through the national Busch Taxidermy Canimal Sweepstakes, fans can win custom "Canimal Taxidermy Trophies," detailed, handcrafted mounts made from Busch Light cans and transformed into iconic hunting trophies. Fans can enter the sweepstakes online.

item.title: Soros nephew divulges how family's power helped bankroll El-Sayed's education during secretive fundraiser
item.description: Jeffrey Soros revealed his role in launching Abdul El-Sayed's career at a secretive Hollywood fundraiser where attendees were asked not to record.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Jeffrey Soros, the wealthy nephew of billionaire Democrat mega-donor George Soros, detailed his yearslong connection to Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed during a Monday night fundraiser, according to footage obtained by Fox News Digital.

The Soros nephew, a wealthy Hollywood producer, hosted El-Sayed at his home Monday night for a fundraiser that attracted controversy given the emphasis the candidate has placed on getting money out of politics. During remarks, Soros noted that he played a key role in helping El-Sayed get his career off the ground, according to footage obtained by Fox News Digital. 

"I just wanted to welcome you here and express my appreciation for coming. And it's been a privilege," Soros said while standing next to El-Sayed during the event, the footage showed. "Speaking of privilege, I've had the pleasure of knowing Abdul since 2012. I got to interview him as a finalist for my parents. Fellowship, the Paul and Daisy Soros Fellowship for New Americans."

The El-Sayed campaign and the Los Angeles Media Fund, where Soros serves as CEO, did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

DEM INSURGENT TURNS ON THE CHARM WITH PARTY ESTABLISHMENT AS SCHUMER LEAVES BITTER FEUD HANGING

Attendees were asked not to record the event, a common practice at many political fundraisers, organizers said in footage reviewed by Fox News Digital.

The Paul and Daisy Soros Fellowship for New Americans, which is designed to help immigrants and the children of immigrants get a leg up in the United States, pays out tens of thousands of dollars in stipend and tuition support to winners. El-Sayed won the fellowship in 2012, and it is touted on its website as one of its success stories.

MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL CALLS AIPAC DONATIONS 'LEGALIZED BRIBERY,' REMAINS SILENT ON OTHER DONATIONS

The financial and political ties come as El-Sayed has made the influence of wealthy donors a recurring theme of his campaign.

"The fundamental corruption of our politics has been the system that allows corporations and would-be oligarchs and billionaires to buy politicians," El-Sayed said during a 2025 local news interview.

"I want to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, pass Medicare for All," he said during a follow-up interview.

A flyer promoting the Soros fundraiser, which was attended by Hollywood notables, stated that attendees could donate up to $57,800 to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, Fox News Digital previously reported. The Soros family’s political machine has also dumped millions into political committees that are supporting El-Sayed’s run for Senate.

SOROS NETWORK REBUILDS PROGRESSIVE PROSECUTOR PUSH AFTER STRING OF ELECTION LOSSES

"Abdul El-Sayed raising dark Soros money in California after begging Chuck Schumer for money in DC is the least surprising thing he’s done all cycle," Alyssa Brouillet, communications director for GOP nominee Mike Rogers' campaign, previously told Fox News Digital. "That’s what a conman does — says one thing and does another. Michiganders can’t trust this guy."

El-Sayed’s campaign has defended itself by arguing that "corporate special interests are spending millions of dollars in dark money to try to buy Rogers a Senate seat because he’s spent his entire career making himself and his billionaire donors richer while Michiganders pay the price."

item.title: ICE confusion ignites MAGA backlash: ‘I would have called for impeachment’
item.description: Verbal guidance telling some ICE offices to stop arresting illegal immigrants without criminal histories was rescinded within hours amid fierce backlash.
item.content:encoded:
Reported guidance directing some ICE offices to pull back on arrests of illegal immigrants without criminal histories triggered backlash from policy hawks, raising questions whether the Trump administration is sending conflicting signals on enforcement.

The guidance was rescinded within hours, and Trump told Fox News there had been no change in an enforcement posture that prioritizes — but is not limited to — the "worst first." The verbal guidance had been relayed to ICE field offices around the country, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter, though it remains unclear who initially issued the instruction.

Administration officials later characterized it as a misunderstanding rather than a formal policy change, and new guidance reaffirming there had been no change in enforcement policy was sent within hours. The episode nevertheless reinforced concerns among some immigration hawks who say recent public messaging from administration officials has suggested a narrower approach to interior enforcement than Trump campaigned on.

Mike Howell, a leader of the Mass Deportation Coalition and president of The Oversight Project, argued public criticism helped force the reversal but said the episode also fit what he views as a broader pattern of mixed messaging from DHS on interior immigration enforcement.

"[The guidance] was walked back, allegedly, which is great, and I think it was in large part walked back because people spoke out very, very loudly," Howell said, while adding there is a troubling undercurrent to some of DHS' messaging on the greater matter:

WHITE HOUSE BRINGS RECEIPTS AFTER MEDIA CLAIMS NONCRIMINAL ICE ARRESTS ‘SOARING’: ‘FALSE NARRATIVES’

As an example, Howell pointed to a tweet from DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin posted one day before the ICE guidance news broke, in which the secretary said the department was "not conducting worksite operations in Kansas" but was targeting criminal illegal immigrants and those facing removal.

The post followed ICE operations in Kansas that prompted complaints from Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., who said DHS had failed to coordinate with local authorities during operations in cities including Liberal.

"I've never seen a secretary put anything like that in writing," Howell said. "[If it were] an Obama or Clinton or Biden DHS secretary, we would have called for impeachment if they said that."

'GONE TOO FAR:' GOP CANDIDATE RUNS TO TRUMP’S LEFT ON SIGNATURE ISSUE IN DEEP RED DISTRICT

Asked to put a finer point on it, Howell stated outright: "If Mayorkas tweeted that, I would have immediately called for his impeachment: for flagrant admission that they are not enforcing the laws and faithfully executing them -- It was amnesty by another means."

Howell emphasized that he was not calling for Mullin’s impeachment, but using the comparison to underscore how seriously he views any pullback from broad immigration enforcement.

He further argued that shifting signals are unfair to rank-and-file ICE agents who served during the Biden administration.

It remained unclear who originated the guidance, but Fox News was told it was a "misunderstanding" and that the person responsible would likely face reprimand.

A source told Fox News Digital on Sunday evening that the order "definitely went out" and that some immigrant-heavy Republican districts have seen anger over family members being caught up in worksite-enforcement removals. The source pointed to Kansas as an illustration.

"This type of ping-pong is deeply unfair to ICE, the men and women there tasked with actually deporting these people," he said. "They watch the news, they read X, they see these mixed signals and it's affected operations."

EXCLUSIVE: DHS SECRETARY MULLIN SLAMS SANCTUARY POLITICIANS AS ATTACKS ON ICE OFFICERS SKYROCKET

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis pushed back, saying Trump has been clear that "no one is off the table."

"DHS continues to deliver results for the American people including the most secure border in history and three straight months of a record number of ICE arrests," she said, citing more than 3 million deportations thus far.

An ICE report also put arrests-per-month at a record high of 51,000 in August, while a source familiar confirmed that ICE guidance that went out was a "miscommunication" and not from the top.

Mark Krikorian, executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies, which advocates for tighter immigration controls, said the situation is uniquely instructive because it comes at a time when factions of the Republican Party are at odds, whether silently or not, over the immigration enforcement issue.

"All of this comes on the backdrop of conflicting goals and messages within the administration on immigration," he said.

Krikorian said the administration may have contributed to that confusion by repeatedly emphasizing its focus on the "worst of the worst," even as officials including border czar Tom Homan have said immigrants without criminal records are not exempt from enforcement.

"The administration does need to get its story straight internally so that they can then present a consistent message externally," Krikorian said.

He argued the larger unresolved issue is worksite enforcement, which he said is critical to encouraging self-deportation but creates political tension between business interests seeking labor and working-class Republicans demanding tighter enforcement.

Republican donors who favor the "loose labor market" that low-wage migrants bring clash with the working-class Republican bloc demanding tighter labor markets and stricter enforcement, Krikorian said.

Krikorian said he had hoped Trump or Mullin would clarify after the Kansas controversy that the administration was not "randomly" cracking down on employers, but conducting worksite enforcement based on intelligence about businesses employing illegal immigrants.

Several Republicans, including Marshall and Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., have criticized aspects of the administration’s immigration push ahead of the midterms. Krikorian argued that conflicting signals could also carry political consequences with Trump voters focused on enforcement – citing competing pressures between big-business and the base.

"You don’t tweet out that you’re not doing what voters want you to do," he said.

Krikorian praised the administration’s border policies but argued interior and worksite enforcement create more complicated political tradeoffs for the Trump coalition.

After the Wire report broke, DHS responded in part "this is false. No one is off the table."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Fox News Digital reached out to Salazar and DHS for further comment.

Fox News' Bill Melugin contributed to this report.

item.title: Which college football coaches improved or tanked their hot seat status four games into the season?
item.description: Lincoln Riley's USC tenure lacks a College Football Playoff appearance through five years, and a home loss to Oregon has the heat rising fast.
item.content:encoded:
If you're not in a headspace to receive sensitive information then plug your ears, but the college football season is officially a third of the way through.

As hard as that is to believe, it also means that we have some significant data to draw from that will help paint a clearer picture of the landscape of college football for 2026.

Some teams are already outperforming their preseason expectations while others are greatly disappointing thus far, as is the case with every season.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL WEEK 4 CONTENDERS, PRETENDERS: TEXAS SURVIVES, MICHIGAN'S KARMA AND COACHES ARE SWEATING

With that, we also have four games worth of data on head coaches and where they stand on the "hot seat" conversation, so I thought it would be interesting to look at a few coaches who entered 2026 with a target on their back and how they've done to either improve or worsen their standing.

Think of it as a "hot seat report card."

KEEP AN EYE ON THESE UNDER-THE-RADAR NAMES DURING THIS SEASON'S COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHING CAROUSEL

With all the preamble out of the way, let's begin.

Dave Aranda's path at Baylor has been a circuitous one, to say the least.

It was looking like a classic rags to riches story for the former LSU defensive coordinator early on, as he guided the Bears to a Big 12 championship and a 12-win season in just his second year on the job.

Since then, the results have fluctuated between middling and downright putrid, and entering this year, Aranda was said to be on his last leg.

So far, though, I don't really think he's done anything to change that for better or for worse, but he has set himself up nicely to buy a little more time in Waco.

Outside of a neutral site opener against Auburn, in which the Bears had a chance to win on the last play even with a hobbled DJ Lagway, Baylor has taken care of business and is 3-1 through four weeks.

Their next few conference games are winnable though not automatic, which sets up an absolutely brutal last three games where they have to play BYU, Texas Tech, and Houston, essentially the best the Big 12 has to offer.

If he can hold serve and maybe even steal one of those three games at the end of the year, I believe 8-4 or 9-3 will land Aranda in the "safe for now" category as 2026 comes to a close.

Status: Hold

Coming into the season, it was basically a forgone conclusion that Wisconsin head coach Luke Fickell would be gone by the end of the year; essentially a dead man walking.

After getting blasted pretty handily by Notre Dame to start the season, it looked like nothing would change, and maybe he's still gone by the end of the year, but Saturday's massive win on the road against a top-15 Penn State might go a long way in determining Fickell's fate.

It was the Badgers' first road win over a ranked opponent under Fickell, and with a more manageable schedule - Wisconsin avoids having to play Indiana, Oregon, and Ohio State this season - a bowl game could be well within range for their embattled head coach.

RANKING THE TEN BEST COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHES IN THE COUNTRY AHEAD OF THE 2026 SEASON

I'm not confident simply making a bowl game will save Fickell, but an 8-4 record is certainly on the table and I'm sure that would give boosters some pause about paying his nearly $20 million buyout.

It's still "wait and see" for Fickell, but Saturday might have been his first attempt at digging out of a massive hole in Madison.

Status: Trending slightly up

This might surprise a lot of people who just paid attention to the preseason polls, but Lincoln Riley was under a lot of scrutiny heading into his fifth year in Los Angeles.

The Trojans have yet to make a College Football Playoff under Riley's watch, causing some of the natives in Southern Cal to stir a bit.

This was seen as the year it could all come together for USC and Riley, and after holding serve the first few weeks of the season, their week four showdown with Oregon was supposed to be the first test of that theory.

Consider that test failed, as the Trojans dropped one at home to a Ducks squad playing with a backup quarterback for the majority of the contest.

Losing to a stacked Oregon team in a vacuum is nothing to hang your head about, but the fact that this was supposed to be a Playoff season for USC means the magnifying glass gets brought out after every result.

There's still plenty of season left to get it right, but things aren't getting any easier for Riley and the Trojans with teams like Ohio State, Penn State, Indiana, and a resurgent UCLA still on the schedule.

Until USC can wash the taste of this one out of their mouth, the temperature on Riley's office chair will feel uncomfortably warm moving forward.

Status: Trending down

It could be argued that no one had a hotter seat coming into 2026 than Mike Norvell, and the Florida State Seminoles didn't exactly do anything to change that through the first third of the season.

The Noles are 2-2 through four games, and their two losses might actually be more inspiring than their two wins.

A three-point home loss to then-ranked SMU and a competitive road loss to Alabama might signify progress, but the fans in Tallahassee have long run out of patience.

Luckily for Norvell and unfortunately for those fans, they don't make the decisions, and after firing athletic director Mike Alford a few weeks ago, the prevailing theory coming out of the Florida panhandle is that their coach is likely safe for 2026.

That might seem almost unfathomable to anyone familiar with the last few years of FSU football, but there's still the lingering questions of Norvell's buyout now coupled with a new AD trying to get his footing in an absolute mess of a situation.

The Seminoles still have a shot at a winning season and a bowl game, and there is some talent at spots on this roster.

I wouldn't be shocked at all to see the Noles pull a 6-6 or 7-5 season out of their hats and keep their lame duck coach in Tally for another season.

I'm sorry, FSU fans. Even you don't deserve a fate this cruel.

Status: Hold

Back in July, I wrote an article about the hot seat status of every coach in the SEC, and South Carolina coach Shane Beamer's seat was so radioactive that it needed its own section all by itself.

Not to toot my own horn, but that is looking downright prophetic four games into the 2026 season.

The Gamecocks took care of the two scrubs on their schedule to start the year before getting their tail feathers handed to them in back to back weeks to begin SEC play.

First, the world was finally introduced to the magic of Mississippi State's Kamario Taylor, as the Bulldogs hung a 41-spot on South Carolina's head in Williams Brice Stadium.

Then Beamer and his boys went on the road and got clobbered by Alabama to the tune of a 49-18 beatdown.

What's worse, their best player, edge rusher Dylan Stewart, had a generational crashout on the field and was sent to the locker room with his status with the team in question, prompting many to opine whether Beamer had "lost the locker room."

Regardless of what becomes of the Stewart situation, the schedule doesn't lighten up at all for South Carolina.

Kentucky, Florida, Tennessee, Oklahoma, and Georgia all await in conference play, and the Gamecocks also have to travel to Clemson to play the Tigers to end the season.

A schedule like that presents opportunities to land some impressive wins, but it also acts as a minefield that could sink the goodship Beamer in the process.

I have a hard time seeing Beamer surviving this season barring a miracle from above.

item.title: Motorcycle patrols swarm Iranian cities, checkpoints rise as regime braces for unrest
item.description: Sources told Fox News Digital that IRGC, Basij and police have flooded Tehran with checkpoints and patrols as student protests over compulsory hijab grow.
item.content:encoded:
Iranian security forces have stepped up their presence in Tehran and other cities, with motorcycle patrols, checkpoints and forces positioned across major urban areas as authorities brace for possible unrest, multiple sources inside Iran told Fox News Digital.

The security buildup comes as university students have returned to the streets in Tehran, protesting compulsory hijab rules, rising education costs and political repression, videos published on Iran International show.

Sources inside Iran confirmed to Fox News Digital that motorcycle units have been operating across Tehran and other cities during events surrounding Iran’s annual "Sacred Defense Week," while members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Basij and law enforcement have been positioned at major squares and other locations.

IRAN INSTALLS NEW WAR CHIEFS AS TEHRAN SIGNALS ‘PROLONGED CONFRONTATION,’ EXPERT WARNS

The sources also said security personnel have stopped pedestrians, searched some individuals and examined mobile phones, including material authorities consider "anti-regime."

The accounts follow a report from the National Council of Resistance of Iran’s (NCRI's) Committee on Security and Counterterrorism alleging that Iranian authorities ordered a "100%" state of readiness for the Army, IRGC, Basij and law enforcement and canceled leave through Sept. 27. The NCRI also claimed 51,000 personnel had been deployed across Greater Tehran, including 30,000 IRGC and Basij members and 21,000 law enforcement personnel. The reported preparations are taking place as signs of public unrest have begun resurfacing on university campuses. Fox News Digital has not independently confirmed those claims.

One source in Tehran told Fox News Digital that the heightened security presence extends beyond what is visible on the streets. 

INSIDE TEHRAN: IRANIANS DESCRIBE IRGC'S BRUTAL RULE, POVERTY — ASK TRUMP TO 'STAY THE COURSE'

"Motorcyclists taking photos of shops, and prisoners being threatened and forced to tell their families not to physically participate in any protests that might arise," the source said.

The source said Basij members who previously received military training have been placed on alert and are being housed or assembled at educational facilities and large properties on the outskirts of Tehran.

The measures were not limited to the capital. "This situation exists in all cities, but the nature of the presence and the way things are organized differ," the source told Fox News Digital, citing information received from Borujen, Isfahan and other cities.

IRAN ACCELERATES EXECUTION CAMPAIGN AGAINST ANTI-REGIME ACTIVISTS AMID INTERNET CENSORSHIP

"In those places, plainclothes agents are more prevalent and try to remain out of public view; however, in Tehran, they appear openly on the streets in military uniforms and gear specifically to instill fear and terror," the source said, adding that leave had also been canceled in smaller cities and claimed shops, telephone communications and everyday activities were under increased surveillance.

Iranian journalist Mehdi Ghadimi, who lives outside Iran after years of opposition activity, separately told Fox News Digital that he had received similar accounts.

"I’ve received reports of new checkpoints being set up in Tehran, and there have also been reports of military forces being put on alert, as well as civilians who had previously been trained by the regime for urban repression being called up," Ghadimi added that people are being detained on espionage charges simply because they communicate with people outside of Iran.

IRAN INMATES SEW LIPS SHUT IN MASS HUNGER STRIKE AT NOTORIOUS US-SANCTIONED JAIL: REPORT

Ghadimi also said he had received reports that individuals with serious criminal records had been released from prison in exchange for reporting to local Basij bases and participating in the suppression of demonstrations.

Students at Allameh Tabataba’i University in Tehran held a protest Monday against compulsory hijab, rising tuition and university living conditions, according to videos reported by Iran International on Sept. 28 and 29. Students were recorded chanting against the morality police and political repression.

Iran International reported that the protest began over tuition, dormitory and food costs before expanding into broader political chants. The outlet, citing the student publication Amirkabir, reported that Basij members attempted to disrupt the gathering and threatened students.

IRAN'S REGIME CAME FOR TEENAGE TWINS. THEIR FATE OFFERS A GLIMPSE OF TEHRAN'S WIDENING DEATH CAMPAIGN

The protests also come amid renewed pressure over compulsory hijab rules on university campuses. On Sept. 8, Iran International reported that a senior official in the office representing Iran’s supreme leader at universities said a new compulsory-hijab directive for universities had been drafted and was expected to be issued by the ministries overseeing higher education.

Separately, the IRGC escalated its rhetoric toward Washington on Tuesday, with spokesman Hossein Mohebbi calling on Americans to pressure President Donald Trump’s administration. "This lying administration must be changed," Mohebbi said at a Tehran press conference, according to Reuters video distributed Sept. 29.

His remarks came as U.S. and Iranian officials continued indirect contacts through mediators in an effort to end the seven-month conflict, Reuters reported.

The combination of visible security preparations and renewed demonstrations is fueling speculation among Iranians about whether the country could face another broader wave of unrest.

"The reality is that nobody knows what’s going to happen," Ghadimi told Fox News Digital. "Everyone I talk to says that this situation cannot continue and that, somehow, it has to come to an end."

item.title: Trump unveils America.gov as AI-powered hub for passports, Medicare enrollment and more
item.description: President Donald Trump launched America.gov, an AI-powered site that consolidates federal services from passport applications to Medicare enrollment in one place.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday unveiled America.gov, an AI-powered website designed to consolidate information from tens of thousands of federal webpages into a single searchable database.

After delivering brief remarks at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, D.C., Trump signed an executive order that directs all federal agencies to make their websites "integrate directly" with America.gov as soon as possible.

The site is live as of Tuesday and allows users to type questions into a search bar that generates AI chatbot-style responses.

"Anyone who has used Grok or Gemini or ChatGPT will understand instantly how to use America.gov," Trump said.

TRUMP ANNOUNCES NEW 'AI FORCE,' VOWS TO PROTECT INDUSTRY AS AI CZAR ANNOUNCEMENT NEARS

Currently, the site can only answer questions and direct users on how to complete various tasks themselves.

U.S. Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia, who helped create America.gov, said that by 2027, citizens will be able to use the site to complete government forms and track the status of various applications.

In his speech, Trump highlighted several ways the site could streamline interactions with the federal government, including simplifying the paperwork involved when a woman changes her last name after getting married.

"Very soon, all she'll have to do is ask America.gov and it'll fill out the forms, track the progress and send her a new Social Security card, passport and insurance card in the mail," Trump said.

UNITED ARAB EMIRATES PLANS AI-RUN GOVERNMENT WITHIN TWO YEARS

"Whether you're a scout leader who wants to reserve a campsite at a national park, a senior citizen trying to choose a Medicare plan, or an American veteran trying to get the benefits that you've earned and so justly deserve, America.gov will be there to help," he added.

Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz followed Trump's remarks with a demonstration of how America.gov could simplify prescription ordering and other services.

Oz brought a woman named Lisa onstage who said she had spent more than a year trying to enroll in Medicare before revealing her newly issued beneficiary card on a large banner.

Oz said America.gov "explains what applies to Lisa's situation and guides her through the decisions."

At the same event Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that beginning in 2027, Americans will be able to use America.gov to apply for their first U.S. passport.

"Today, if you need your first passport, you start at the State Department's website," Rubio said. "There's a lot of information up there, but if you actually want to apply, that is where the maze starts."

Rubio said the site will allow users to upload their own passport photos, eliminating the need to visit a pharmacy or retail store to have one taken.

"No printing forms, no drugstore hostage photo, no appointment, no line, no middleman that you're paying to do something that should be available to you," Rubio said. "You tell America.gov what you're trying to do and it walks you through every single step."

More federal services are expected to be added over the coming months as agencies begin to integrate with America.gov.
